title: German grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday fluency, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is everyday Standard German as people speak it in Germany.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first German conversation.
lessons.topic: {{ich bin}}, {{ich heiße}}, {{ich komme aus}}; the two words for “you”: {{du}} and {{Sie}}

goal.t: Hallo, ich heiße Anna. Ich komme aus Kanada.
goal.tr: Hello, my name is Anna. I'm from Canada.

dialog.t: Ich komme aus Kanada. Und du?

blocks.p: Three ways to say who you are, all usable today: {{Ich bin Jonas.}} “I'm Jonas.”, {{Ich heiße Anna.}} “My name is Anna.” (word for word “I am called Anna”), and {{Ich komme aus Kanada.}} “I come from Canada.”

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Canada.
a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, she, it.
a word for an action or a state: come, live, be, want.

blocks.p: **I.** {{ich}} is “I”. Unlike English “I”, it has no capital letter, except at the start of a sentence. When you talk about yourself, most verbs end in {{-e}}: {{ich heiße}}, {{ich komme}}, {{ich wohne}} “I live”. {{ich bin}} “I am” is the odd one out.

**You: du or Sie.** German has two words for “you”. {{du}} is for friends, family, children, and people your age in a relaxed setting. {{Sie}} (always with a capital S) is for strangers, shop staff, your boss: anyone you'd call Mr. or Ms. The verb changes with them:

ex.note: said by a woman; a man says {{Lehrer}}. With jobs, German leaves out “a”.

ex.t: Guten Tag, ich bin Frau Weber.
ex.note: {{Guten Tag}} is the polite hello during the day
most countries need no “the”: {{aus Kanada}}, {{aus Spanien}}; a few do: {{aus den USA}}, {{aus der Schweiz}}

blocks.tip: {{ß}} is a German letter for a sharp “ss” sound: {{heißen}} sounds like “HY-sen”. And when you're not sure whether to say {{du}} or {{Sie}}, say {{Sie}}: people will offer you {{du}} if they want it.

mistakes.why: {{heiße}} already means “am called”, so there's no room for {{bin}}. Say {{Ich bin Anna}} or {{Ich heiße Anna}}.
With {{du}}, the verb ends in {{-st}}. {{-en}} is for {{Sie}}.
For your job, German says just the job, with no word for “a”.

practice.q: You're talking to a hotel receptionist you've never met. “You” is…
practice.why: A stranger at work: {{Sie}}. {{du}} is for friends, family and children.
With {{ich}}, the verb ends in {{-e}}: {{ich komme}}.

practice.q: You're Tom, from London. Choose your replies.

lines.why: About yourself: {{ich}}. {{du heißt}} would be “your name is”.

practice.q: Ask a friend: “Where are you from?”
Your turn: say hello, your name and where you're from. Start with {{Hallo, ich heiße…}}

answers.t: Hallo, ich heiße Sarah. Ich komme aus England.
answers.tr: Hello, my name is Sarah. I'm from England.

answers.t: Hallo, ich bin David. Ich komme aus Kanada und wohne in München.
answers.tr: Hi, I'm David. I'm from Canada and I live in Munich.

lessons.title: Ask someone about themselves
lessons.summary: Ask where someone lives, what they do and which languages they speak, and understand the answers.
lessons.topic: Question words ({{wer, was, wo, woher, wie}}); verb endings {{-e}}, {{-st}}, {{-en}}; the verb in second place

goal.t: Wo wohnst du und was machst du beruflich?
goal.tr: Where do you live and what do you do for a living?

dialog.tr: Mia. Where do you live, Ben?

dialog.t: Ich wohne in Köln. Und du?
dialog.tr: I live in Cologne. And you?

dialog.t: In Bonn. Was machst du beruflich?
dialog.tr: In Bonn. What do you do for a living?

blocks.means: a word that asks for information: who, what, where, how.

table: {{Was machst du?}} What are you doing?
{{Wo wohnst du?}} Where do you live?
{{Woher kommst du?}} Where are you from?

blocks.p: **The verb comes second.** This is the most important rule of German word order: in a sentence that tells or asks for information, the verb is the **second** thing. In a question, the question word is first and the verb comes right after it: {{Wo wohnst du?}}, word for word “Where live you?”. English needs “do” (“Where *do* you live?”); German never does: the verb itself moves up.
It's the second *thing*, not always the second word: in {{Mia und ich wohnen in Bonn.}}, “Mia and I” is one thing, and {{wohnen}} comes after it. You'll meet this rule in every lesson.

blocks.means: the basic form of a verb, the one in the dictionary: {{wohnen}} “to live”, {{machen}} “to do, to make”. In German it almost always ends in {{-en}}.

blocks.p: **Endings.** To use a verb, take the infinitive, drop {{-en}}, and add the ending for who's doing it: {{-e}} for {{ich}}, {{-st}} for {{du}}, and {{-en}} (the same as the infinitive) for {{Sie}}.

ex.t: Was lernst du? – Ich lerne Deutsch.
ex.tr: What are you learning? – I'm learning German.

ex.note: short for {{Wie geht es dir?}}; to a stranger: {{Wie geht es Ihnen?}}

blocks.tip: If a verb's stem ends in {{-t}} or {{-d}}, an extra {{e}} makes it easy to say: {{du arbeitest}}, {{du findest}}. If it ends in {{-s}}, {{-ß}} or {{-z}}, {{du}} adds only {{-t}}: {{du heißt}}.

mistakes.why: After a question word, the verb comes second: before {{du}}.
{{-en}} is for {{Sie}}; with {{du}}, the verb ends in {{-st}}.

practice.q: Which one asks a friend “Where are you from?”
practice.why: {{woher}} asks “where from”, and the verb comes second. ({{wer}} means “who”.)

practice.tr: What do you do for a living?
Where do you live? – In Munich.
practice.why: The answer is a place, so the question word is {{wo}} “where”.

lines.tr: And what do you do for a living?

lines.why: A statement: {{ich}} first, then the verb in second place.

practice.q: Ask a friend: “How old are you?”
Your turn: you've just met someone. Ask them two things, with {{du}} or {{Sie}}.

answers.t: Wo wohnst du? Und was machst du beruflich?
answers.tr: Where do you live? And what do you do for a living?

answers.t: Woher kommen Sie? Welche Sprachen sprechen Sie?
answers.tr: Where are you from? Which languages do you speak?

lessons.title: Talk about other people
lessons.summary: Introduce a friend and say where people live and what they do: “This is Lena. She's from Vienna.”
lessons.topic: {{er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie}}; the whole present of regular verbs and of {{sein}} “to be”

goal.t: Das ist Lena. Sie kommt aus Wien und wohnt jetzt in Berlin.
goal.tr: This is Lena. She's from Vienna and lives in Berlin now.

dialog.tr: Hi Lena! Where are you from?

blocks.p: **Das ist…** “This is…” or “That is…” introduces anyone: {{Das ist Lena.}} {{Das ist Herr Becker.}}
Here is every person a verb can have. The endings follow a pattern, and {{sein}} “to be” is irregular, as “be” is in English:

Two things make it easier than it looks. {{wir}}, {{sie}} “they” and {{Sie}} “you” always share one form, which is the infinitive for every verb except {{sein}}. And {{er/sie/es}} and {{ihr}} both end in {{-t}}.

**sie, sie and Sie.** {{sie}} is “she” and also “they”; {{Sie}} with a capital is the polite “you”. The verb tells you which: {{sie wohnt}} “she lives”, {{sie wohnen}} “they live” (or, with a capital, “you live”).
**ihr** is “you” for two or more people you'd each call {{du}}: friends, family, children. For one stranger or several, it's {{Sie}}.

ex.t: Er heißt Paul und arbeitet in Hamburg.
ex.tr: His name is Paul and he works in Hamburg.

ex.t: Das ist Herr Becker. Er ist Lehrer.
ex.tr: This is Mr. Becker. He's a teacher.

blocks.tip: {{Herr}} is “Mr.” and {{Frau}} “Ms.” or “Mrs.”, with the last name: {{Herr Becker}}, {{Frau Weber}}. Someone you call that, you call {{Sie}}.

mistakes.why: One person (she): {{-t}}. {{-en}} is for we, they and the polite you.

options: “They live in Berlin” or “You live in Berlin” (polite)
practice.why: “She lives” is {{sie wohnt}}. With {{wohnen}}, it's “they” or the polite “you”: the situation (and in writing the capital S) tells them apart.
{{wir sind}} “we are”. {{seid}} goes with {{ihr}}, {{ist}} with one person.
One person: {{-t}}, with an extra {{e}} after the {{t}} of {{arbeit-}}.

practice.q: Introduce your friend Marco to Ms. Schulz.

options: Guten Tag, Frau Schulz! Das ist Marco.
Guten Tag, Frau Schulz! Das sind Marco.

practice.q: Your turn: introduce a friend or someone in your family: their name, where they're from, where they live. Start with {{Das ist…}}

answers.t: Das ist Tom. Er kommt aus London und wohnt in Berlin.
answers.tr: This is Tom. He's from London and lives in Berlin.

answers.t: Das ist Maria. Sie ist Ärztin und wohnt in Madrid.
answers.tr: This is Maria. She's a doctor and lives in Madrid.

lessons.title: Ask yes-or-no questions and say no
lessons.summary: Ask “Are you…?” and “Do you…?”, answer yes or no, and say what isn't so.
lessons.topic: The verb first in yes/no questions; {{nicht}} “not”; {{ja}}, {{nein}} and {{doch}}

goal.t: Wohnst du hier? – Nein, ich wohne nicht hier.
goal.tr: Do you live here? – No, I don't live here.

dialog.tr: Excuse me, is this seat free?

dialog.t: Danke. Fahren Sie auch nach Köln?
dialog.tr: Thanks. Are you going to Cologne too?

dialog.t: Nein, nach Bonn. Wohnen Sie in Köln?
dialog.tr: No, to Bonn. Do you live in Cologne?

dialog.t: Nein, ich wohne nicht in Köln. Ich besuche dort meine Schwester.
dialog.tr: No, I don't live in Cologne. I'm visiting my sister there.

blocks.p: **The verb first.** For a question you answer with yes or no, put the verb at the very start: {{Du wohnst hier.}} “You live here.” becomes {{Wohnst du hier?}} “Do you live here?” Again, no “do”: the verb itself moves to the front.
So German has two kinds of question. With a question word, the verb is second; without one, the verb is first:

**nicht** “not” comes after the verb, never before it. Put it at the end of the sentence, or before a place ({{nicht hier}}, {{nicht in Köln}}) or a describing word ({{nicht müde}}): {{Ich komme nicht.}} {{Ich wohne nicht hier.}} {{Er ist nicht müde.}}

**ja, nein, doch.** {{ja}} is “yes” and {{nein}} “no”. German has a third answer English doesn't: {{doch}} is “yes” as the answer to a question with “not” in it, when you disagree with it: {{Kommst du nicht? – Doch!}} “Aren't you coming? – Yes, I am!”

ex.t: Kommen Sie aus Österreich? – Nein, aus der Schweiz.
ex.tr: Are you from Austria? – No, from Switzerland.

ex.t: Arbeitet Paul heute? – Nein, heute nicht.
ex.tr: Is Paul working today? – No, not today.

ex.t: Kommst du heute nicht? – Doch, natürlich!
ex.tr: Aren't you coming today? – Yes, of course I am!

blocks.tip: As in English, a statement with a rising voice is also a question: {{Du kommst aus Kanada?}} “You're from Canada?”

mistakes.why: {{nicht}} comes after the verb, never between {{ich}} and the verb.

mistakes.wrong: Kommst du nicht? – Ja, ich komme!
mistakes.right: Kommst du nicht? – Doch, ich komme!
mistakes.tr: Aren't you coming? – Yes, I am!
mistakes.why: To say “yes” against a question with {{nicht}}, use {{doch}}.

practice.q: A friend asks {{Bist du nicht müde?}} “Aren't you tired?” You are tired. You say…
practice.why: You disagree with the “not” in the question, so it's {{doch}}. {{Nein}} would mean “No, I'm not tired.”
“Not” in a sentence is {{nicht}}; {{nein}} is the answer “no”.

practice.tr: Where do you live? – In Cologne.
practice.why: The answer is a place, so the question word is {{wo}}, and the verb comes right after it.

practice.q: On the train: answer the woman next to you.

lines.tr: Excuse me, are you going to Munich?

options: Nein, ich fahre nicht nach München.
Nein, ich nicht fahre nach München.

lines.why: {{Ja}} stands outside the sentence; then comes a normal statement: {{ich}}, then the verb.

practice.q: Ask two friends: “Are you from Spain?”
Your turn: someone asks you {{Wohnst du hier?}} Answer, then ask them a yes-or-no question back.

answers.t: Nein, ich wohne nicht hier. Wohnst du hier?
answers.tr: No, I don't live here. Do you live here?

answers.t: Ja, ich wohne hier. Und du, kommst du aus Berlin?
answers.tr: Yes, I live here. And you, are you from Berlin?
